name: What is Equilibrium?
what: This subtopic introduces the distinction between reversible and irreversible reactions and explains what it means for a reaction to reach dynamic equilibrium. It also clarifies the difference between the rate of a reaction and the extent of a reaction.
why: Understanding equilibrium is foundational to the rest of the topic. Without a clear grasp of what dynamic equilibrium means and how it differs from a stopped reaction, students will misapply Le Chatelier's principle and make errors in both calculations and written explanations.

items.title: I can state the difference between reversible and irreversible reactions
items.what: A reversible reaction can proceed in both the forward direction (reactants to products) and the reverse direction (products back to reactants). An irreversible reaction proceeds in one direction only and cannot be undone.
items.why: This distinction is essential before studying equilibrium, because equilibrium only applies to reversible reactions. Knowing which type of reaction you are dealing with determines whether equilibrium concepts are relevant at all.
items.example: Burning wood is irreversible - once the wood is ash you cannot turn it back. The reaction N2(g) + 2O2(g) = 2NO2(g) is reversible, indicated by the double half-arrow, meaning NO2 can also decompose back to N2 and O2.

items.title: I can explain the difference between rate of reaction and extent of reaction
items.what: Rate of reaction describes how quickly reactants are being converted to products (change in concentration per unit time). Extent of reaction describes how far the reaction has proceeded toward completion, based on the relative concentrations of reactants and products at a given moment.
items.why: These two concepts are often confused. A reaction can have a high rate but low extent (quick reaction that barely converts reactants), or a slow rate but high extent. Separating them is necessary for analysing and optimising industrial chemical processes.
items.example: In the reaction H2(g) + I2(g) = 2HI(g), the rate tells you how fast HI is being produced per second. The extent tells you whether, at equilibrium, mostly HI or mostly H2 and I2 are present - a large K value would indicate a high extent.

items.title: I can define dynamic equilibrium
items.what: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a closed reversible reaction where the forward and reverse reactions are occurring at the same non-zero rate, so the concentrations of all species remain constant over time.
items.why: The word 'dynamic' is critical - it means the reaction has not stopped. Students frequently describe equilibrium as the reaction stopping or concentrations becoming equal, both of which are incorrect. Precise language here is directly assessed in VCE examinations.
items.example: In the sealed system N2O4(g) = 2NO2(g), at equilibrium the brown colour of NO2 remains steady. This does not mean the reaction has stopped - NO2 molecules are still combining to form N2O4 at the same rate that N2O4 is decomposing into NO2.

items.title: I can describe the characteristics of a homogeneous equilibrium system
items.what: A homogeneous equilibrium is one where all reactants and products are in the same phase (for example, all gases or all aqueous). The system must be closed, the forward and reverse rates must be equal, concentrations must be constant, and a mixture of both reactants and products must be present.
items.why: All equilibrium systems encountered in VCE Chemistry Unit 3 are homogeneous. Knowing the defining characteristics allows students to correctly identify when a system is at equilibrium and avoid common misconceptions about what 'constant concentration' means.
items.example: The reaction Fe3+(aq) + SCN-(aq) = FeSCN2+(aq) is a homogeneous aqueous equilibrium. At equilibrium, the deep red colour of FeSCN2+ stays constant, indicating that all three species are present at stable, unchanging concentrations in the one phase.
